Lesson 7 · Business route

From prediction to intervention

Would offering a new team tool improve performance?

The business problem

A team-performance manager sees that users of a new tool outperform nonusers and is asked to fund a wider rollout. Managers chose the first recipients, so the observed gap includes both the tool’s contribution and the starting differences between teams. The budget question is more precise: would offering the tool to eligible teams improve performance enough to cover licenses, training, and disruption?

What the data show

Teams that received the tool exceed others by 15.08 outcome units in the observed data. That raw gap mixes selection and treatment.

The user-versus-nonuser average is a useful signal to investigate, but it is not the gain the purchase would create. The manager needs to define the offer, the team unit, the performance measure, and the period before comparing outcomes. A pilot that randomly offers the tool to some eligible teams gives a clearer comparison with usual operations. Track actual use as a separate implementation measure, since the decision to offer a tool and the decision to use it answer different questions.

What would you decide?

Define who should receive the offer and what outcome matters. Random assignment, when feasible, makes the offered and usual-operation groups comparable on average.

Set a minimum gain per team that would repay the rollout cost. Assign the offer among eligible teams, keep the assignment list, and measure the same outcome on the same schedule for both groups. Report the result by offer, plus adoption and training effort. If the gain clears the threshold, expand in stages; if adoption is weak, improve implementation before buying for the whole organization.

Pause and explain

Can the observed treated–untreated gap be reported as the tool effect?

Compare your reasoning

No. Teams were selected partly for characteristics related to their outcomes. The gap includes a baseline difference.

Check your judgment

Reveal the case’s known answer

The generator stores both potential outcomes. Its average effect among recipients is 4.58; its average effect across all teams is 2.42. Those are different targets.

The bigger picture

A business can predict which teams will do well and still be uncertain whether buying a tool will help them. The purchase decision calls for a comparison of what happens with and without an offer, tied to a budget threshold. A planned pilot makes that comparison part of the rollout rather than an afterthought. The wider lesson applies to training, software, incentives, and service changes: define the intervention and the gain needed to justify it before expansion. The next lesson tackles the same decision when an experiment was not built into the program.
